title.narrative: IWRM 4 WASH A Market-based Approach

description.narrative: Inception phaseIn year one (October 2019-July 2021), the project will undertake a number of activities geared towards setting a strong foundation for effective project implementation. Key activities that will be prioritized during this phase include defining the project scope and gaining stakeholder consensus; developing a detailed implementation plan with the key strategic partners, conducting a baseline assessment to establish the project benchmarks; developing a project risk and mitigation plan, handling all logistical and administrative requirements and exemptions necessary for smooth project implementation and setting up the monitoring and evaluation system. - This phase would pursue the case study, action-learning, and networking components in parallel. Implementation phaseImplementation of the anticipated follow-up project (component 2) is estimated to take four years (July 2021 - December 2025). The outputs of activities for component one (the inception phase) will determine the extent and scope of the second phase of the Project. Hence, the detailed activities needing external funding will be further defined after the end of the first phase.

Integrated Water Resources Management for Water Sanitation and Hygiene is a Market-based approachThe project will be implemented in Ethiopia, focusing on the water catchment areas surrounding Addis Ababa in the Oromia Regional State. It will specifically target the four main surface water supply sources for Addis Ababa: the Legedadi, Gefersa, Dire, and Akaki catchments, along with their associated reservoirs. Additionally, the project will extend to five nearby towns within and around these catchment areas: Akaki, Burayu, Gelan, Sululta, and Sendafa.

name.narrative: Upper Awash Basin – Oromia and Addis Ababa (Dire, Adere, Legedadi, Sululta, Sendafa, Gelan, Akaki)

description.narrative: The IWRM4WASH project operates across the Upper Awash Basin, mainly within Oromia Regional State and Addis Ababa’s water catchment zones. The program integrates water resource management, WASH service expansion, and livelihood initiatives. Core intervention areas include Adere and Legedadi catchments for watershed rehabilitation; and the towns of Sululta, Sendafa, Gelan, Akaki, and Burayu for improved water and sanitation services.

activity-description.narrative: Between 2021 and 2024, the project implemented a mix of watershed rehabilitation, WASH infrastructure construction, and utility capacity development. Key outputs include the rehabilitation of 925.7 ha of degraded land, sediment reduction by 30%, construction of reservoirs and sanitation facilities benefiting over 165,000 people, and digitalization of utility billing systems. Activities are implemented through VEI in partnership with AAWSA, OWERDB, and local utilities.

policy-marker.narrative: Gender equality and women’s participation were mainstreamed across project activities.Women represented about 45 % of training participants and over 50 % of irrigation and catchment groups.Gender-sensitive WASH infrastructure (separate and disability-friendly toilets) was implemented in Sendafa and Gelan.

The project directly contributes to climate-change adaptation by promoting integrated watershed management, soil and water conservation, and reforestation that reduce erosion and strengthen ecosystem resilience inthe Upper Awash Basin.
The project strengthens governance through trans-regional dialogue between AAWSA, OWERDB, and MoWIE, and by empowering local utilities and communities in joint watershed and WASH planning.

Improved reservoir protection and catchment rehabilitation through IWRM interventions

description.narrative: Between 2021 and 2024, the IWRM4WASH project implemented large-scale SWC interventions in the Adere (Dire) and Legedadi catchments to protect key water-supply reservoirs for Addis Ababa and Sheger towns.A total of 925.7 ha of degraded land (≈ 89 % of the 1,037 ha target) was rehabilitated through terraces, check-dams, gully treatments, and biological measures such as grass planting and afforestation. The 2024 Hectare Verification Report validated this figure.According to the 2024 Erosion Control Study, annual soil loss in the Adere watershed decreased from 185,911 t (2021) to 130,075 t (2024) — a 30.03 % reduction, far exceeding the project’s 5–10 % goal. Biological interventions planted over 208,000 seedlings, and the construction of a masonry dam with solar-powered irrigation system created jobs for 30 youth while enhancing local agricultural productivity.Implementation was guided by joint planning between AAWSA, OWERDB, BoA, and local watershed committees, ensuring strong ownership and integration into the Upper Awash catchment management framework.

title.narrative: In 2024, substantial progress was achieved in the Adere watershed (Dire catchment) through Soil and Water Conservation (SWC) interventions.A total of 378.14 hectares of degraded land were treated — 112.5% of the 2024 annual target — bringing the cumulative treated area to 925.7 ha, equivalent to 89% of the 1,037 ha overall project goal.Findings from the 2024 Hectare Verification Report confirmed that all rehabilitated sites were physically verified and geo-referenced using GPS and GIS mapping tools, ensuring accuracy and traceability.The verification, jointly conducted by VEI, AAWSA, local watershed experts, validated the rehabilitation achievements reported through physical measurement and visual inspection of SWC structures and vegetative cover.

title.narrative: IWRM4WASH Project Annual Narrative Report 2024

description.narrative: In 2024, the IWRM4WASH project entered its fourth year, advancing integrated water, sanitation, and watershed management across the Upper Awash Basin.It supported over 125,000 people in Akaki, Burayu, Gelan, Sululta, and Sendafa, protecting vital water sources for Addis Ababa.Under IWRM, 378.14 ha of land were rehabilitated (112.5% of the target), with masonry dam construction and biological restoration transforming degraded areas.Over 208,000 seedlings were planted, reinforcing soil and water conservation and creating jobs through community-led fruit farms.Key WASH achievements include functional reservoirs in Gelan, Sendafa, and Sululta, benefiting 65,000 people with reliable water access.New sanitation blocks at schools and markets improved hygiene for over 26,000 students and residents.Overall, 2024 demonstrated how integrated watershed restoration, livelihood development, and resilient WASH services can jointly drive sustainable change.Overall: Verified cumulative results up to Dec 2024: 165,750 people with improved WASH access; 925.7 ha rehabilitated (89% of 1,037 ha target); utilities operationalised; cross-cutting achievements.

description.narrative: This indicator measures the cumulative reduction in annual soil loss and sediment export within the IWRM4WASH intervention catchments (mainly Adere watershed under the Dire and Legedadi systems).It reflects the combined environmental impact of physical and biological soil and water conservation (SWC) measures — such as terraces, check dams, reforestation, and grass planting — implemented between 2021 and 2024.Sediment reduction contributes directly to reservoir protection and water security for Addis Ababa and surrounding towns.The values are derived from RUSLE and InVEST erosion-modelling tools, verified through the 2024 Erosion Control Study and compared against baseline conditions from 2021.

title.narrative: Expanded access to safe water and sanitation services in Burayu, Sululta, Sendafa, Gelan, and Akaki through improved utility capacity and inclusive infrastructure.

description.narrative: From 2021–2024, IWRM4WASH expanded safe water, sanitation, and community infrastructure across the Upper Awash Basin, focusing on Burayu (2022), Sululta (2023), Sendafa (2024), Gelan (2024), Bura Maru (2024), and Akaki (ongoing 2025). These interventions enhanced access to clean water, improved sanitation services, and supported inclusive community development.Key Achievements (2021–2024):Burayu (2022): Commissioned a 500 m³ concrete reservoir and constructed a 16-seat public market toilet block in Sebeta. The system included the provision and installation of submersible pumps and improved distribution pipelines. Together with Sululta, these 2022 completions provided safe water access to an estimated ~70,000 people that year.Sululta (2023): Completed a 500 m³ reservoir benefiting 20,000 people in Kombolcha Kebele. The system was connected to the Sululta TWSSSE network, expanding reliable water supply coverage and strengthening utility service delivery.Sendafa (2024): Completed a 300 m³ reservoir, ~6 km pipeline, and a 16-seat public toilet block (including 2 disability-friendly units), benefiting 25,750 people. The project was inaugurated in March 2024 and supports improved sanitation and hygiene access for local market users and nearby communities.Gelan (2024): Constructed a 500 m³ reservoir and a 12-seat school toilet block at Dambi Gara Primary School, serving 25,000 residents and 532 students. Final electrical and connection works are ongoing and expected to be completed in early 2025.Bura Maru (2024): Constructed a crossover structure (small bridge) serving four kebeles and improving access for approximately 12,000 people to health centers, markets, and social facilities. This structure enhances mobility, economic integration, and climate resilience in the area.Akaki (2024–2025): Implementation began with 30% completion of a 200 m³ reservoir, 25% progress on a 10-seat toilet block, and the start of pipeline installation. The project is expected to benefit 15,000 people upon completion in 2025.Utilities and Service Efficiency: Digital billing and customer management systems were deployed in Sululta, Sendafa, and Gelan, enhancing operational efficiency, billing accuracy, and revenue collection, contributing to long-term utility sustainability.By December 2024, cumulative WASH access reached ≈165,750 people (Burayu, Sululta, Sendafa, Gelan, and Bura Maru completed; Akaki ongoing).These interventions not only improved service delivery but also strengthened local utility capacity, promoted gender- and disability-inclusive sanitation access, and enhanced resilience through integrated infrastructure.

title.narrative: ABC of Watershed Management

description.narrative: From 2021–2024, cross-cutting measures under IWRM4WASH ensured inclusivity, sustainability, and adaptive learning across all components.The project integrated gender equity, youth participation, climate resilience, and knowledge sharing into both watershed and WASH interventions.Key Achievements (2021–2024):Gender Equality:Maintained gender balance across trainings and consultations (≈ 45 % women participants).Gender considerations embedded in design of sanitation facilities (e.g., separate male/female blocks, two disability-friendly units in Sendafa).Youth Engagement:Over 30 youth employed through the Dire masonry dam fruit-farm livelihood pilot.Young experts at Woreda level actively contributed to GIS mapping, data management, and erosion-modelling studies.Knowledge Management:Three knowledge briefs and technical papers produced (IABC of Watershed Management, erosion modelling, and hectare verifications).Collaboration with local universities facilitated research theses on watershed management and climate impacts.Findings from RUSLE and InVEST SDR erosion modelling (2021–2024) disseminated during EKN review and Embassy briefings.Climate and Resilience:Completed climate impact analysis identifying vulnerabilities in the Dire and Legedadi catchments.Modelled soil-loss reduction (30 % cumulative decrease 2021–2024) validating effectiveness of SWC measures.Recommendations integrated into ongoing IWRM planning and trans-regional policy dialogue.Cross-cutting actions reinforced inclusivity, evidence-based learning, and sustainability, directly supporting SDG 5, 6, and 13 commitments.

title.narrative: Livelihoods and food security enhanced through adaptive, community-based approaches supporting catchment restoration and access improvement.

description.narrative: The livelihood component of the IWRM4WASH project was initially designed to pilot a market-based approach by linking conservation incentives to microfinance-supported enterprises.However, due to limited engagement from local MFIs and logistical constraints, this component was not implemented as originally envisioned.Instead, the project adopted an adaptive livelihood model integrated with watershed rehabilitation efforts. Between 2021 and 2024, the following practical results were achieved:Establishment of a fruit farm and nursery enterprise at the masonry dam site, creating daily employment for 30 youth.Distribution of 6,000 fruit seedlings for homestead planting, improving household nutrition and small income potential.Engagement of local farmers and community groups in soil-fertility management, tree planting, and maintenance of rehabilitated areas.Completion of a crossover structure connecting four kebeles, benefiting approximately 12,000 people with better access to markets, schools, and health facilities.Although the formal market-based component and full training program (targeted at 1,000 individuals and 100 ha improved farmland) were not completed, the project’s adaptive interventions contributed to sustained livelihoods, local employment, and improved mobility for rural communities.

title.narrative: Strengthened trans-regional dialogue and coordination for Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) in the Upper Awash Basin

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of multi-stakeholder trans-regional dialogue meetings conducted in 2024 to strengthen coordination between Addis Ababa Water and Sewerage Authority (AAWSA), Oromia Water and Energy Resources Development Bureau (OWERDB), Basin Development Authority (BDA), and other key institutions engaged in Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM).In 2024, one high-level Trans-Regional Dialogue was successfully convened in Addis Ababa.The meeting brought together over 40 representatives from federal and regional agencies to review catchment management progress, align IWRM-WASH integration priorities, and agree on next-year action plans for joint watershed protection.The discussion reaffirmed institutional collaboration commitments and set the groundwork for finalizing the Strategic Framework for Trans-Regional Cooperation.

title.narrative: Number of trans-regional dialogue meetings conducted in 2024

description.narrative: This indicator tracks the number of high-level trans-regional dialogue meetings convened in 2024 to strengthen coordination between Addis Ababa Water and Sewerage Authority (AAWSA), Oromia Water and Energy Resources Development Bureau (OWERDB), Basin Development Authority (BDA), and other key institutions working on Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) in the Upper Awash Basin.In 2024, one high-level trans-regional dialogue was successfully conducted in Addis Ababa.Although the original logframe envisioned two dialogues per year, this proved overly ambitious given the executive nature of the meetings, which require cross-institutional scheduling, approvals, and high-level representation.To maintain momentum, the project organized multiple mid-level stakeholder forums and technical consultations throughout the year. These sessions engaged over 60 experts and decision-makers from federal, regional, and utility institutions to review project progress, share IWRM best practices, and align planning for watershed rehabilitation, WASH integration, and policy coordination.The 2024 dialogue reaffirmed institutional collaboration and strengthened consensus around the Strategic Framework for Trans-Regional Cooperation, which is being finalized for joint adoption in 2025.

title.narrative: Institutional collaboration and trans-regional dialogue established for integrated water resource management.

description.narrative: The IWRM4WASH project strengthened cooperation among AAWSA, OWERDB, MoWIE, Basin Development Authority (BDA), BoA, Sheger City Administration, and VEI to promote coordinated catchment management across administrative boundaries.During the inception phase (Dec 2020), a baseline validation workshop was convened that brought these key institutions together for the first time to validate the biophysical and socio-economic baseline results and to agree on shared IWRM priorities. This meeting laid the foundation for formalized trans-regional coordination under Result 1.Between 2021 and 2024, regular technical consultations and stakeholder fora were conducted to maintain coordination and share progress. In 2024, one executive-level trans-regional dialogue was successfully held, engaging all major institutions and EKN, leading to joint understanding of IWRM–WASH linkages and commitments for sustained collaboration.

comment.narrative: During the inception phase (Dec 2020), a baseline validation workshop was convened that brought these key institutions together for the first time to validate the biophysical and socio-economic baseline results and to agree on shared IWRM priorities. This meeting laid the foundation for formalized trans-regional coordination under Result 1.Between 2021 and 2024, regular technical consultations and stakeholder fora were conducted to maintain coordination and share progress. In 2024, one executive-level trans-regional dialogue was successfully held, engaging all major institutions and EKN, leading to joint understanding of IWRM–WASH linkages and commitments for sustained collaboration.

The original plan for two dialogues per year was adjusted due to the high-level nature of these events.One executive-level trans-regional dialogue was held in 2024 (AAWSA, OWERDB, MoWIE, BoA, Sheger City, EKN).Four additional technical and stakeholder fora were organized between 2022 and 2024.The 2020 baseline validation workshop (inception phase) served as a foundation for these formal dialogues but is not included in the numeric count.Continuous coordination through technical fora ensured the intended policy alignment and cooperation objectives were achieved.
